Setting up apt-get to use a http-proxy

These are three methods of using apt-get with a http-proxy.

Temporary proxy session

This is a temporary method that you can manually use each time you want to use apt-get through a http-proxy. This method is useful if you only want to temporarily use a http-proxy.

Enter this line in the terminal prior to using apt-get (substitute your details for yourproxyaddress and proxyport).

```
export http_proxy=http://yourproxyaddress:proxyport
```

If you normally use sudo to run apt-get you will need to login as root first for this to work unless you also add some explicit environment settings to /etc/sudoers, e.g.

```
Defaults env_keep = "http_proxy https_proxy ftp_proxy"
```

APT configuration file method

This method uses the apt.conf file which is found in your /etc/apt/ directory. This method is useful if you only want apt-get (and not other applications) to use a http-proxy permanently.

Low Resolution Icons and OS Features

If you have problems with low resolution icons, shortcuts and menus placed strangely, and especially desktop size not matching your monitor, this may be due to a bug with multiple monitor setup. If you've previously setup a second monitor and have it plugged in but not turned on, Ubuntu/Xubuntu may be counfounded by this. The simplest method to resolve this is to remove the redundant cable from your machine and reboot. Additionally, install arandr (GUI for xrandr editing) and setup two profiles, one with the secondary monitor and one without. Removal of redundant cable when not in use is nonetheless still recommended. This problem was experienced in Ubuntu and Xubuntu.

Screen Blanks/Monitor Turns Off

Using a laptop with a GeForce Go card, or connecting the sole display via DVI on a dual-head system sometimes results in the screen not receiving a picture. This is caused by the driver outputting video to the VGA port on the graphics card, instead of DVI.

input.text: No rush, but How do I add the option acl to the partition s on which? Thanks for any help you can offer.
input.subject: Add the option acl to the partition s on which

expected.answer:
by default.

```
$ sudo apt-get install acl
```

1) Add the option acl to the partition(s) on which you want to enable ACL in /etc/fstab. For example:

```
...
UUID=07aebd28-24e3-cf19-e37d-1af9a23a45d4 /home ext4 defaults,acl 0 2
...
```

As of Ubuntu 14.04 and for ext4, the above is not required as acl are already default:

```
sudo tune2fs -l /dev/sdaX |grep acl
Default mount options: user_xattr acl
```

2) If necessary, remount partition(s) on which ACLs were enabled for them to take effect. For example:

```
$ sudo mount -o remount /home
```

3) Verify that ACLs are enabled on the partition(s):

```
$ mount | grep acl
```

ACL Entries

ACL entries consist of a user (u), group (g), other (o) and an effective rights mask (m). An effective rights mask defines the most restrictive level of permissions. setfacl sets the permissions for a given file or directory. getfacl shows the permissions for a given file or directory.

Defaults for a given object can be defined.

ACLs can be applied to users or groups but it is easier to manage groups. Groups scale better than continuously adding or subtracting users.

Listing ACLs

You add `acl` to the **mount options** for the filesystem you want to use ACLs on. First find which filesystem contains the directory in question. For example, for `/home`:

```bash
findmnt -no SOURCE,FSTYPE,TARGET /home
```

Then inspect its entry in `/etc/fstab`:

```bash
sudoedit /etc/fstab
```

An entry might look like:

```text
UUID=...  /home  ext4  defaults  0  2
```

If ACLs are not already enabled and that filesystem needs the option, add `acl` to the fourth field—the mount options—separated by a comma:

```text
UUID=...  /home  ext4  defaults,acl  0  2
```

Keep the existing options; don’t replace the UUID, filesystem type, or other fields. Save the file, then remount that filesystem (replace `/home` with its actual mount point):

```bash
sudo mount -o remount /home
```

On modern Ubuntu installations using **ext4**, ACL support is normally enabled by default, so you may not need to change `/etc/fstab` at all. You can check whether the ACL tools are available with:

```bash
getfacl /home
```

If that command is missing, install them with `sudo apt install acl`. If you share the output of `findmnt -no SOURCE,FSTYPE,TARGET /home` and the relevant `/etc/fstab` line, I can help identify exactly what—if anything—you need to change.

e Ubuntu installer, you need to make sure you have an EFI System Partition (ESP) set up. This partition holds EFI-mode boot loaders and related files.

If your disk already contains an ESP (eg if your computer had Windows 8 preinstalled), it can be used for Ubuntu too. Do not format it. It is strongly recommended to have only 1 ESP per disk.

An ESP can be created via a recent version of GParted (the Gparted version included in the 12.04 disk is OK), and must have the following attributes:

Mount point: /boot/efi (remark: no need to set this mount point when using the manual partitioning, the Ubuntu installer will detect it automatically)

Size: minimum 100Mib. 200MiB recommended.

Type: FAT32

Other: needs a "boot" flag.

Wrong again. A NAT router is a great addition to your security, but as I've been enforcing throughout this post, that there is no catch all solution. A NAT router will prevent a service from being bound and accessible from the Internet. That being said, it works a lot like strong inbound only rules as we discussed earlier in this post. When used in conjunction with the other topics we've discussed in this post a NAT router is an excellent hardening measure, however as a stand alone solution it is lacking in many ways. Replace each placeholder with details supplied by your network administrator. For example, if they give you proxy host `proxy.example.com`, port `8080`, username `alice`, and password `secret`, the address would look like:

```text
http://alice:secret@proxy.example.com:8080/
```

Remove the angle brackets—don’t type `<username>` literally. If the proxy doesn’t require a username and password, use:

```text
http://proxy.example.com:8080/
```

For APT, an example `/etc/apt/apt.conf.d/80proxy` file would be:

```text
Acquire::http::Proxy "http://proxy.example.com:8080/";
Acquire::https::Proxy "http://proxy.example.com:8080/";
```

Many proxies use the same `http://` address for HTTPS traffic; use the exact format your administrator provides. You generally don’t need an FTP entry.

**Don’t guess the proxy host or port.** If you don’t know them, ask your workplace/school IT team. Also, proxy passwords stored in these files are plain text. If your password contains characters such as `@`, `:`, or `/`, it may need URL-encoding; ask IT for the correct format rather than putting your normal password in directly.
